goals: Quantify the effect of soil clay content on runoff vs recharge partitioning in a controlled setting
key_processes: Infiltration capacity decline with increasing clay content
Hydraulic conductivity control on subsurface drainage vs surface runoff

model_choice.rationale: ELM's soil hydraulic parameterization directly represents clay-content control on infiltration and drainage. A controlled single-column experiment isolates this mechanism by varying only clay content while holding forcing, vegetation, and location fixed.

answerable: Clay-content control on infiltration vs runoff partitioning
Monotonic response of partitioning to clay gradient

sampling_strategy.n_justification: Six clay-content levels (5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, 45%, 55%) span the requested range and resolve the partitioning response curve. Each level is one column with uniform synthetic soil. No replication needed for first-order mechanism isolation.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Not spatial — all columns at the same arbitrary CONUS location to ensure identical forcing and eliminate spatial confounders.
sampling_strategy.replication: None — single column per treatment suffices for controlled mechanism isolation

sampling_plan.reason: Sandy soil (5% clay): high infiltration, minimal runoff, maximum recharge — lower bound of clay range
Loamy sand (15% clay): moderate infiltration, beginning of runoff increase
Loam (25% clay): balanced partitioning, mid-range hydraulic conductivity
Clay loam (35% clay): reduced infiltration, increased runoff dominance
Clay (45% clay): low hydraulic conductivity, runoff-dominated partitioning
Heavy clay (55% clay): minimal infiltration, maximum runoff, minimal recharge — upper bound of clay range

validation_design.observation_source: Literature expectations (Rawls et al. hydraulic property tables, infiltration theory)
validation_design.comparison: analog — compare partitioning trends to published hydraulic-conductivity vs clay-content relationships
validation_design.metric: Monotonic trend verification: runoff fraction should increase and recharge fraction should decrease with clay content
validation_design.n_validation_points: Not applicable — validation is against physical expectation, not point observations

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: Uniform synthetic soil at each clay level, single representative CONUS location, 1990-2000 forcing period (10-year climatology), uniform grassland vegetation

requires_capabilities.why: Need to create six columns with controlled clay content (5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, 45%, 55%) and uniform sand/silt partitioning, independent of SSURGO spatial data
requires_capabilities.blocks: Ability to isolate clay-content effect without spatial soil heterogeneity confounders

requires_capabilities.why: Need to average over interannual forcing variability to obtain stable partitioning statistics and allow soil moisture to reach quasi-equilibrium
requires_capabilities.blocks: Robust partitioning estimates — single-year runs would be dominated by that year's precipitation anomaly

assumptions: Sand and silt fractions are adjusted proportionally to maintain 100% total texture for each clay level
Vegetation type (PFT distribution) is held constant across all treatments
Forcing location is arbitrary but within CONUS NLDAS-2 coverage to ensure valid meteorology
10-year simulation period is sufficient to average interannual variability and reach quasi-equilibrium partitioning
ELM's default soil hydraulic parameterization (likely Clapp-Hornberger or van Genuchten) adequately represents clay-content effects on infiltration and drainage
open_questions: Should sand/silt be partitioned in a specific ratio (e.g. constant sand:silt) or allowed to vary to match standard texture-class definitions?
Is there a preferred forcing period or location to maximize precipitation variability and test partitioning under diverse wetness conditions?
Should we include a brief spin-up (e.g. 2 years) before the 10-year analysis period to stabilize soil moisture, or is cold-start acceptable for a relative comparison?
